full_judgment:
Ruhul Islam J.—This appeal by special leave arises from an application under section 14 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 filed by respondent No. l in respect of certain land with the Dacca City. The sale under pre-emption was effected by Ayesha Khatun respondent No. 2 in favour of the appellant by a kabala dated 10-9-73 which was registered on 5-4-76. The case land appertained to a permanent tenure recorded in C.S. Khatian No. 214 under Mouza Shahar Dacca, owned by Akshoy Kumar SahaBanik, and Rangubala Choudhurani. Akshoy Kumar SahaBanik instituted Title Suit No. 126 of 1946 in the First Court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca for partition and by the decree passed in the suit Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik got 1/3rd share and Ran-gubala got the remaining rd share. One Nafisa Khatun by purchasing the interest of Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik by a registered deed of sale dated 19-7-52 became co-sharer of Rangubala. Rangubala created a lease in respect of her 2/3rd share for 99 years by a registered deed of lease dated 23-12-53 in favour of Ayesha Khatun, respondent No. 2 Nafisa Khatun sold her interest to respondent No. 1 by a registered sale deed dated 18-4-72. Ayesha Khatun also sold her interest to the appellant by a registered sale deed dated 10-9-73. Against this sale respondent No. 1 filed the application for pre-emption. The appellant contested the case by filing written objection contending, inter alia, that the respondent No. 2 was not a co-sharer in the tenancy, because the land of the tenure was partitioned by the decree in Title Suit No. 126 of 1946 between Akshoy Kumar Saha Banik and Rangubala Choudhurani ; and that a separate tenancy was created in favour of Ayesha Khatun by Rangubala by granting permanent lease for 99 years, reserving for herself annual rent of Tk. 1/-; and that Ayesha Khatun paid rent of Tk. 1/- to the lessor Rangubala till the rent receiving interest was acquired by the Government; and that S.A. Khatian was not correctly prepared because neither respondent No. 1 nor his vendor was co-sharer of Ayesha Khatun. He further claimed that after his purchase he applied for mutation of his name and accordingly his name was mutated in the S A. Khatian and jama was separated. The learned Subordinate Judge allowed pre-emption case against the appellant and the appeal was dismissed. Thereafter the appellant moved the High Court Division in revision under section 115(1)1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and being unsuccessful moved this Court and obtained leave from this Court to appeal from the judgment of the High Court Division. 

 4. According to section 18 the Revenue-officer is required to prepare or revise the record-of-rights in pursuance of the order passed under section 17, and in preparing or revising the record-of-eights the Revenue- officer has been directed to record such particulars as may be prescribed under the Rules. Rule 18 quoted above shows that the nature of the particulars to be recorded as provided in clause (b) of rule 18 the Revenue officer is required to record the class or the classes to which each tenant or occupant belongs, whether the tenant is a proprietor, tenure holder, raiyat holding at fixed rates, settled raiyar, occupancy raiyat, non-occupancy raiyat, under raiyat, with or without a right of occupancy, or a non-agricultural tenant, and if he is a tenure-holder, whether be is a permanent tenure-bolder or not, and whether his rent is liable to enhancement during the continuance of his tenure, Clause (f) requires that rent payable at the time the record-of-rights is being prepared as well as the rents determined as fair and equitable according to rules 28 to 30 to be mentioned. Rule 24 provides for preparation of preliminary record-of-rights which is also known as draft record-or-rights. According to this rule, the draft record shall consist of statements of rights which are styled as the khatians. This rule further directs that ordinarily there shall be a separate khatian for each person interested, or each group of persons jointly interested, in the land, whether as proprietor, tenure-holder, raiyar, under-raiyat, occupant or non-agricultural tenant and each khatian shall show the rights and liabilities of each person or group of persons. Statutory provisions clearly show sections 18 and 19 and the rules 18, 19 and 24 do not support the proposition canvassed by the learned Advocate on the elimination of the rent receiving interests all under-raiyats became raiyats under the Government and their status having thus been upgraded, the Revenue-officer while preparing the record-ofrights was required to record the under-raiyat as a raiyat in separate khatian, fixing fair and equitable rent for such upgraded tenant. It has already been stated above that the preparation of record of rights as provided in section 17 was with a view to assessment of compensation payable for all such interests liable to be acquired under the Act. Rule 24 provides for preparation of statements of rights which is styled as the khatian. According to this rule ordinarily there shall be a separate khatian for each person interested or each group of persons jointly interested in the land whether as proprietor, tenure-holder, raiyat, under-raiyat, occupant or non-agricultural tenant and each khatian shall show the rights and liabilities of each person or group of persons, according to particulars mentioned in rule 18. The rules neither authorize nor require the Revenue-officer to prepare separate khatians for the individual raiyats and under-raysts, but, on the other hand, it provides that each group of person jointly interested in the land, whether as proprietor, tenure-holder, raiyat, under raiyat, occupant or non-agricultural tenant ordinarily are to be shown in separate khatian, and it further provides that each khatian shall show the rights and liabilities of each person or group of persons, recording the particulars as indicated in rule 18. In support of the proposition that the under raiyat was upgraded to the status of raiyat, on the elimination of rent receiving interest, support was sought from the doctrine of merger as provide in section 22 of the Bengal Tenancy Act which provides that when the raiyati disappears the under-raiyat cannot any longer remain as such. Section 22 as it stands after amendment of 1907 merely provides that 08 the transfer of the occupancy right to a person jointly interested in the land as proprietor or permanent tenure-holder, such person shall have no right to hold the land as the raiyat but shall hold it as a proprietor or permanent tenure-holder as the case may be. By the amendment of 1907 the principle of merger as contemplated in section 22 was altered. The most important incident of merger under sub-section (1) of section 22 is that the landlord does not hold the land upon merger as a raiyat but holds it only as a proprietor or a permanent tenure-holder. It necessarily follows that the under-raiyats are automatically promoted to the status of raiyats. This view received judicial recognition in Ram Charan Sutradhar Vs. SM. Makhan, 38 CWN 1976, and it was followed by a Division Bench in the case of Pramatha Nath Shikder Vs. Jitendra Nath Roy. 43 CWN 1102. Upon acquisition of the rent receiving interests all under-raiyats by operation of law became raiyats under the Government is not in controversy, but the doctrine of merger as provided in section 22 of the Bengal Tenancy Act has no application to the conversion of all tenants holding land as proprietor, tenure holder raiyat, under-raiyat, occupant or non-agricultural tenant, as raiyats or maliks under the Government. 

 5. The question boils down to this, whether on the acquisition of the rent-receiving interest, that is, the interest of Akshoy and Rangubala Choudhurani the under-raiyati created by the latter by executing permanent lease dated 23-12-63 for 99 years in favour of Ayesha Khatun, respondent No.2, stood upgraded to that of a raiyat and the statute recognizes the upgraded under-raiyat as raiyat for all practical purposes. The khatian was rightly prepared in accordance with rule 18, recording the under-raiyat of Ayesha Khatun without changing its status. Rule 18 provides that while preparing the record-of-right the Revenue-officer concerned shall record the class or classes to which each tenant or occupant belongs, that is, occupancy raiyat, non-occupancy-raiyat, under raiyat, etc. There is nothing in rule 18, which requires the Revenue-officer to record the under-raiyat as the upgraded raiyat in the khatian. It is in evidence that the S. A. Khatian was prepared by the Revenue-officer under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act recording Akshoy Kumar Saba Banik and Rangubala Cboudhurani as raiyats and Ayesha Khatun as under raiyat, and Jama of Tk. 10/- fixed under the Bengal Tenancy Act remaining the same. According to Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, in the S. A. Khatian prepared after the whole sale acquisition of rent-receiving interests Rangubala Choudhuraoi could not be shown as a raiyat in the khatian, and the khatian showing Rangubala Choudhurani as a raiyat was wrong According to him. Ayesha Khatun should have been shown as a raiyat. In support of his argument reliance was placed on a decision of the Dacca High Court in the case of Mubasher Ali V. Md. Mokbul Hossain, 19 DLR 271 The decision seems to support the argument. The learned Judges expressed their view regarding consequential effect upon existing tenants on the acquisition of all rent-receiving interests under section 3 of the State Acquisition and tenancy Act in the following term: 

 "After the final publication of the Compensation Assessment-roll, the Collector shall assign a tauzi number to all the lands under one tahsil and inform the Revenue-officer accordingly. The Revenue-officer shall, thereafter rearrange the khatians under that tauzi number by eliminating therefrom the entire chain of interests of rent-receivers and showing therein only the "tenants who will come directly under the Provincial Government." 

 37. This appeal arises out of a pre-emption case under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. The land under pre-emption represents 2/3rd share of the original permanent tenure recorded in C S. Khatian No 214 of Dhaka city belonging to '"Bangladesh, the remaining 1/3rd share of which belonged to her co sharer Akshoy Kumar. As both the owners held and possessed the tenure in khas the tenure has been referred to as an occupancy raiyati although by a decree in a partition suit- T.S. No. 126 of 1946, they separately possessed their respective shares. Askhoy transferred his 1/3rd share to one Nafisa Khatun by sale deed dated 19 July, 1952, and Nafisa Khatun on her part transferred the same interest to respondent No. 1, who is the pre-emptor in this case, by a sale deed dated 18 April 1972. As to Rangubala's 2/3rd share, she created a lease in favour of Ayesha. Khatun by a registered lease-deed dated 23rd December 1933 and started realizing rent from her at therate of Re. 1/- a year. Ayesha Khatun sold her land to the appellant who is pre-emptee in this case, by a registered sale-deed dated 10 September 1973, and it is this transfer which has given rise to this pre-emption case. 

 38. Respondent No.1, pre-emptor, has sought pre-emption of the two-third share of the former tenancy under C.S. Khatian No. 214 claiming to be a co-sharer in the tenancy as against the appellant who is a stranger purchaser. He denied the creation of any under-raiyati in favour of Ayesha Khatun by the lease-deed dated 23rd December 1953 (Exhibit E) which is, according to him, an "out and out sale." This claim is resisted on two grounds. One ground is that the Lease-deed is a genuine document creating an under-raiyati interest under Rangubala, and as such the original tenancy stood automatically divided, Rangubala retaining only the rent receiving interest in her two-third share. In view of this under raiyati, it is further contended, Rangubala, the landlord was not a co-sharer of Ayesha, the tenant, in the same tenancy and consequently, Nafisa Khatun, vendor of Respondent No. 1, was not a co-sharer of Ayesha though she was a co-sharer of Rangubala in, respect of the superior interest, namely the occupancy raiyati. The other ground is that by the decree of Partition suit of 1946, the original tenancy was divided between Akshoy and Rangubala who thereupon exclusively possessed their respective shares. 

 40. The main ground urged before us by Khondkar Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Advocate for the appellant, is that the upgrading of the under-raiyati no doubt took place on the acquisition of the rent-receiving interests on April 14, 1956, but this upgrading did not re unite the former under-raiyati with the one- third share of the original tenancy which also became a raiyati under the Government. The upgrading of this under-raiyati resulted in creation of a separate, distinct and independent raiyati having no connection with the raiyati of Nafisa Khatun, vendor of Respondent No.1. In other words, on this 'upgrading' the former share of Nafisa and i share of Rangubala became two independent tenancies. Mr. M. H. Khandkar, learned Advocate for the Respondent contends that the finding of the learned Single Judge that an under-raiyati was created by the Lease Deed is erroneous since the S.A. Khatian did not support the creation of any under-raiyati and the original jama of Rs. 10/- for the entire tenancy also continued to be paid. But it should be noted that presumptive value of record of rights prepared under section 103B of the Bengal Tenancy Act is not attached to a S.A. khatian. Secondly, though the original jama was shown in the S.A. khatian, Respondent No. 1 could not produce any rent receipt for payment of rent at the original rate. Appellant, on the other hand produced rent-receipts showing that Ayesha paid rent to Rangubala and thereafter to the Government in respect of the  share of the former tenancy. As to the Lease-Deed, it is a registered instrument expressly creating a lease under Rangubala. As such I do not find any substance in the contention that no under-raiyati was created.
